relational-fundamentals-and-sql.r: A report double-counted customers because a join matched several rows per customer. Understanding keys and relationships made the cause obvious, and a different join gave correct totals.
relational-fundamentals-and-sql.x: Operators need enough SQL to read plans and spot risky queries. Know what keys and constraints guarantee, and why the database, not the application, should enforce integrity.

indexes-and-query-plans.r: A page became slow as a table grew. The plan showed a full scan; adding an index on the filtered column turned seconds into milliseconds. A later write slowdown reminded the team that every index has a cost.
indexes-and-query-plans.x: Indexes trade write speed and space for read speed. Read the plan, check estimates against reality and remove unused indexes. Beware that plans change as data and statistics change.

transactions-and-locking.r: A long transaction held a lock overnight and other queries piled up behind it until the application stopped responding. Finding the blocking session and setting a statement timeout prevented a repeat.
transactions-and-locking.x: Know your isolation level and what anomalies it allows. Keep transactions short, take locks in a consistent order, and set timeouts so one bad session cannot stall everything.

backups-and-recovery.r: A team had nightly backups for years, and when they needed one, the restore failed because the backup was incomplete. Regular restore tests found that fault before it mattered.
backups-and-recovery.x: A backup is only real once restored. Define recovery point and time, use point-in-time recovery, keep copies in another place and time the restore on production-sized data.

replication-and-failover.r: After a failover, writes were lost because the replica was behind when the primary died. The team learned the difference between asynchronous and synchronous replication and chose based on their tolerance for loss.
replication-and-failover.x: Failover is a distributed systems problem: detection, fencing, promotion and client redirection. Practise it, avoid split brain, and measure replication lag as a first-class signal.

performance-and-connection-pooling.r: A traffic spike opened thousands of database connections and memory ran out. A connection pooler in front of the database kept the number of server connections small and stable.
performance-and-connection-pooling.x: Connections are expensive. Pool them, size from the database's capacity, find slow queries by statistics and watch for noisy neighbours, memory settings and checkpoint behaviour.

safe-schema-migrations.r: A migration that added a column with a default locked a large table for ten minutes during business hours. Splitting it into adding a nullable column, backfilling in batches and then adding the constraint avoided any downtime.
safe-schema-migrations.x: Make schema changes backward compatible in steps: expand, migrate, contract. Test migrations on production-sized data, set lock timeouts and keep a rollback plan for both code and data.

nosql-caches-and-choosing.r: A team chose a document store because it was fashionable and then needed relational queries it could not do well. Starting from access patterns and consistency needs would have guided the choice better.
nosql-caches-and-choosing.x: Choose by data shape, access pattern, consistency and operational skill, not by hype. A cache is not a source of truth; plan for stampedes, invalidation and what happens when it is empty.

postgres-vacuum-bloat-and-maintenance.r: A table grew to ten times its real size because autovacuum could not keep up. Tuning autovacuum for that table and repacking it recovered space and speed.
postgres-vacuum-bloat-and-maintenance.x: Postgres needs maintenance as a design fact. Watch dead tuples, long transactions that block cleanup and transaction ID age, and treat autovacuum settings as part of capacity planning.

schema-design-for-operations.r: A table used a natural key that later changed, and updating it meant touching many other tables. Using a stable surrogate key and proper constraints made later changes much simpler.
schema-design-for-operations.x: Good schemas are easy to migrate, back up and debug. Choose keys, types and constraints deliberately, avoid unbounded growth in a single table and plan partitioning before you need it.

debugging-database-problems.r: The application was timing out. A quick look at active sessions showed one query blocking dozens of others, and ending that session restored service in a minute. The root cause, a missing index, was fixed the next day.
debugging-database-problems.x: Triage in a fixed order: is it up, is it blocked, is it slow, is it full. Mitigate safely, capture evidence such as plans and sessions before killing anything, then fix the cause.
